result: Fat body-specific Dp depletion does not affect muscle development, while muscle-specific Dp depletion results in smaller muscles.
evaluation: Claims C30-C32 are directly supported by quantitative measurements of VL3 muscle area shown in Figure 1A-B. The data clearly demonstrate that cg>Dp-RNAi (fat body-specific) does not alter muscle size, while Mef2>Dp-RNAi (muscle-specific) significantly reduces muscle area, consistent with previous reports (C31).

result: Muscle-specific Dp depletion causes binucleated cells in fat body through a systemic effect, without altering Dp expression in fat body.
evaluation: Claims C34-C55 collectively demonstrate a key systemic effect. The appearance of binucleated cells in fat body of Mef2>Dp-RNAi animals (C40) is well-documented in Figure 2A-B. Critically, Dp levels remain unchanged in fat body of these animals (C49-C50, C53-C54, Figure 3), confirming tissue-specific depletion. The absence of MRN protein recruitment (C42) distinguishes this from cell-autonomous effects, supporting the systemic nature of the phenotype (C43-C44, C55).

result: GAL4 drivers show tissue-specific expression patterns with no leaky expression, confirmed by G-TRACE lineage tracing and Dp::GFP reporter analysis.
evaluation: Claims C45-C53 provide comprehensive validation of tissue specificity using multiple complementary approaches. G-TRACE data (Figure 3A-B) confirms cg-GAL4 expression in fat body only and Mef2-GAL4 in muscles only (C45-C47). Dp::GFP reporter analysis (Figure 3C-G) and anti-Dp immunostaining (Figure 3E, 3H) independently confirm efficient depletion only in targeted tissues (C48-C53). This multi-pronged validation is rigorous and convincing.

result: Muscle-specific Dp expression rescues fat body binucleation in Dp mutants, but fat body-specific expression does not rescue muscle defects, revealing asymmetric inter-tissue communication.
evaluation: Claims C56-C64 demonstrate a striking asymmetry in rescue experiments (Figure 4). Muscle-specific Dp expression (Dp-/-; Mef2>Dp) largely rescues fat body binucleation (C58), though incompletely (C59), while fat body-specific expression fails to rescue muscle size defects (C62-C63). This asymmetry strongly supports the conclusion that E2F/Dp modifies inter-tissue communication (C64). The data are internally consistent and well-controlled.

result: Proteomic profiling reveals extensive changes in Dp-deficient tissues, with shared alterations in carbohydrate metabolism pathways between fat body and muscle.
evaluation: Claims C65-C80 describe comprehensive proteomic analysis identifying 6578 and 5370 proteins in fat body and muscle respectively (C65-C66). The data show appropriate validation of Dp depletion and E2F target upregulation (C67-C68). Functional enrichment analysis reveals significant shared changes in glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, and carbohydrate metabolism (C78-C80, Figure 5D), with correlation r=0.172 between tissues (C70). The statistical approaches (FDR<5%) and multiple validation steps support these conclusions.

result: Metabolomic profiling confirms carbohydrate metabolism defects, with significant reductions in glycolytic intermediates in Dp mutants.
evaluation: Claims C81-C85 present targeted metabolomics data showing 55 significantly changed compounds (C81, FDR<5%). KEGG pathway enrichment identifies glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, and ammonia recycling as significantly affected (C82). Critically, four core glycolytic metabolites are significantly reduced (C83, Figure 5G-H), directly confirming the proteomic predictions. The use of two control strains (Canton-S and w1118) strengthens the conclusions by accounting for genetic background effects.

result: High sugar diet fully rescues lethality of fat body-specific Dp depletion but not muscle-specific depletion, demonstrating tissue-specific metabolic requirements.
evaluation: Claims C86-C96 demonstrate a striking dietary rescue specific to fat body Dp depletion. While cg>Dp-RNAi animals die on control diet (7.9% sugar, C93), survival increases to ~50% at 12% sugar and is fully rescued at 16-24% sugar (C94-C95, Figure 6A). This is confirmed with a second driver (r4-GAL4, C96). In contrast, Mef2>Dp-RNAi survival is unaffected by diet (C87, Figure 6B). The specificity of rescue strongly supports distinct metabolic roles for E2F in different tissues.

result: Fat body-specific Dp depletion reduces circulating trehalose levels, which are restored by high sugar diet, while muscle-specific depletion does not affect trehalose.
evaluation: Claims C97-C101 establish a mechanistic link between Dp loss and trehalose homeostasis. Proteomic data show reduced Tps1 and increased trehalase in Dp-deficient fat body (C97-C98). Direct measurements confirm significantly reduced hemolymph trehalose in cg>Dp-RNAi on control diet (C99, Figure 6D), which is restored by high sugar diet (C100). Mef2>Dp-RNAi shows no trehalose defect (C101, Figure 6E). This tissue-specific metabolic phenotype directly correlates with the rescue pattern.

result: Fat body-specific Dp depletion reduces lipid storage, which is improved by high sugar diet, while muscle-specific depletion does not affect lipid storage.
evaluation: Claims C103-C109 demonstrate fat storage defects in cg>Dp-RNAi. Lipid droplet size is reduced on control diet (C103, Figure 6F), consistent with reduced acetyl-CoA carboxylase expression (C104). High sugar diet improves droplet size (C106) and fully restores triglyceride levels (C107-C108, Figure 6G). Muscle-specific depletion shows no lipid storage defects (C109, Figure 6H). The data are quantitative and statistically significant, supporting the tissue-specific metabolic role of E2F.

result: High sugar diet rescues lethality and metabolic defects but not the binucleated cell phenotype, suggesting distinct mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C111-C114 reveal an important dissociation between phenotypes. Binucleated cells persist in both cg>Dp-RNAi and Mef2>Dp-RNAi on high sugar diet (C111-C112, Figure 6—figure supplement 1H-I), despite complete rescue of lethality and metabolic defects. This strongly supports the inference that binucleation is mechanistically distinct from metabolic dysfunction (C114), representing a separate consequence of E2F loss.

result: E2F loss causes both tissue-intrinsic metabolic changes and systemic effects, with fat body Dp depletion causing low trehalose as the likely cause of lethality.
evaluation: Claims C2-C8 and C115-C150 represent the major conclusions of the work. The manuscript demonstrates that E2F inactivation in either tissue causes lethality (C2), regulates carbohydrate metabolism (C3, C115-C116), and causes both tissue-intrinsic and systemic effects (C8, C147, C150). The dietary rescue experiments (C6-C7, C117) combined with trehalose measurements (C4) strongly support the conclusion that low circulating trehalose is the main cause of cg>Dp-RNAi lethality (C149). The evidence is comprehensive and internally consistent across multiple experimental approaches.

result: Dietary protein and lipid content differentially affect survival of fat body-specific Dp-depleted animals.
evaluation: Claims C89-C92 describe additional dietary manipulations. High protein is detrimental, causing melanotic masses and developmental delay (C89-C90, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, C-D), while reducing protein suppresses these defects (C91). Increasing lipid to 1% improves survival to ~22% adult eclosion (C92). The data are clear, though the mechanisms are not explored in detail. These findings support the general conclusion that cg>Dp-RNAi animals have altered metabolic requirements.

result: Glycogen storage is not significantly affected by Dp depletion in either tissue.
evaluation: Claim C110 reports no major defects in glycogen storage in either cg>Dp-RNAi or Mef2>Dp-RNAi animals on control or high sugar diet (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F-G). This negative result is important for ruling out glycogen metabolism as a major contributor to the phenotype and focusing attention on trehalose and lipid metabolism.

result: Binucleated cells in fat body are associated with DNA damage response in cell-autonomous Dp depletion.
evaluation: Claims C33-C39 describe the cell-autonomous effects of Dp loss in fat body. The binucleated phenotype is observed with multiple drivers (cg-GAL4, Lpp-GAL4) and in E2f1/E2f2 double mutants (C36-C39), confirming it is a consistent feature of E2F loss. The association with DNA damage response (C33) is supported by previous work (Guarner et al., 2017) and confirmed by MRN protein recruitment data in Figure 2C.

result: Muscle-specific Dp depletion causes systemic effects in fat body, possibly through stress-induced paracrine signals.
evaluation: Claims C130-C133 interpret the systemic effects of muscle Dp depletion. The appearance of binucleated cells in Mef2>Dp-RNAi fat body demonstrates systemic effects (C130), though the mechanism differs from cell-autonomous effects due to lack of DNA damage response (C131). The speculation about stress-induced signals (C132) is reasonable given the literature on muscle-fat body communication, though direct evidence for the mechanism is not provided. The conclusion of systemic effects (C133) is well-supported.

result: Tissue-specific Dp knockdown causes extensive proteomic changes, affecting 20% of proteins in fat body and 51% in muscle.
evaluation: Claims C145-C146 quantify the extent of proteomic changes following Dp depletion. These percentages are directly calculated from the proteomic data with appropriate statistical thresholds (FDR<5%, |FC|>1.5). The larger percentage in muscle (51% vs 20%) may reflect the different developmental stages analyzed (pharate vs larva) or genuine tissue differences. This demonstrates that E2F loss has widespread effects beyond cell cycle regulation.

result: The severity of metabolic phenotypes may differ between whole-body and tissue-specific Dp inactivation due to altered metabolic balance.
evaluation: Claims C119, C135-C137 present speculation about metabolic balance in different genetic contexts. While the reasoning is logical—that tissue-specific depletion creates metabolic imbalances not present in whole-body mutants—these claims are not directly tested. The speculation about trehalose demand and supply (C135-C136) is plausible but lacks experimental validation. This represents an interesting hypothesis for future work rather than a demonstrated result.
